title: KPI Dashboards: Funnels & Cohorts
objective: After this lesson you will be able to compute funnel stage conversions with absolute sizing, read cohort tables diagonally and horizontally, and define every dashboard metric with formula + window + exclusions.
why: Dashboards drive weekly decisions on numbers nobody defined: conversion of what over whom, retention of which event, active meaning what? Metric definitions (formula + population + window + exclusions) plus funnel/cohort discipline turn dashboards from wallpaper into instruments — and undefined metrics into arguments nobody can settle.

blocks.text: Each stage shows **conversion rate from previous** (diagnosis: where the cliff is) **and absolute count** (sizing: what fixing it wins). Biggest relative drop × volume = priority. Funnel definitions state windows (checkout within session? 7 days?) and dedup rules (one conversion per user or per attempt?) — same shape, different numbers.

blocks.caption: Stage rates with absolutes: diagnose relatively, size absolutely

blocks.text: **Rows** age one cohort (lifecycle shape); **diagonals** compare same-age across cohorts (true retention shifts vs mix effects). Newcomers read rows only and mistake mix changes for retention changes. Always pair with cohort sizes (small cohorts wobble) and precise event definitions (any order? completed? which window?).

blocks.caption: Two readings, two questions: diagonals for trends, rows for lifecycles

blocks.text: Every metric ships **formula + population + window + exclusions + owner**: 'checkout conversion = unique purchasers / unique product-viewers, 7-day window, excluding staff, owned by growth'. Undefined metrics generate unresolvable arguments ('conversion is down' — which conversion?). Definitions live beside dashboards, versioned with changes.

blocks.title: Rank the drops
blocks.note: Run it: views→carts collapses 77.8% on 900 volume — the cliff to work first. Rates locate (77.8%), counts size (900 at stake): priority needs both numbers.

items: Funnels: stage rates (diagnose) + absolutes (size); priority = drop × volume
Cohorts read rows (aging) + diagonals (true trends) with sizes and event definitions
Metric contracts: formula + population + window + exclusions + owner, versioned

exercise.prompt: (a) Run the practice funnel and confirm the four stage lines + priority. (b) Compute the diagonal averages for cohorts [[0.5,0.3],[0.6,0.4]] (two cohorts, two ages) by hand. (c) Write the conversion metric definition (formula/population/window/exclusions/owner) for checkout.
hints: Lines: visits 100/0, views 90/10, carts 22.2/77.8, checkout 25/75; priority views→carts (rate×volume).
Diagonals: age0 (0.5+0.6)/2=0.55, age1 (0.3+0.4)/2=0.35 — same-age comparison across cohorts.
Definition: purchasers/viewers, 7-day window, exclude staff/test, owner growth (versioned beside dashboard).
exercise.why: Stage math (rates+absolutes), diagonal reading (trends vs lifecycles), and contract writing (five-part definitions) are the three dashboard judgments.
exercise.code: // Dashboard pattern: funnel rates + cohort diagonals + metric contracts.

options: Which conversion? (formula/population/window/exclusions/owner) — undefined metrics generate unresolvable arguments
quiz.explain: Metric contracts precede incident response: definition first, diagnosis second. Arguing undefined numbers wastes the crisis.

quiz.q: Cohort rows improve over time. Conclusion?
options: Check diagonals first: row aging vs same-age comparison — mix effects mimic retention shifts
quiz.explain: Rows age cohorts (lifecycle); diagonals compare same-age across time (true trends). Conclusions need both readings plus sizes.

quiz.q: Funnel stage with biggest drop but tiny volume vs smaller drop, huge volume. Priority?
options: Drop × volume product: rates locate, absolutes size — priority maximizes expected win
quiz.explain: Priority needs both numbers: relative diagnosis times absolute prize. Either alone misallocates effort.

summary: Rates + absolutes in funnels, rows + diagonals in cohorts, five-part contracts on every metric. Dashboards as instruments, not wallpaper.
